title: Family and possession
goal: Name family members, say what you have, and attach the three possessive endings — *-ku*, *-mu*, *-é* — plus see how krama replaces them.
bekal: name family members in ngoko and krama
use *duwé* / *gadhah* to say what you have
replace *-ku* and *-mu* with *kula* and *panjenengan* in krama

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Ngobrol karo Rini bab kulawarga
dialogs.intro: First night at the boarding house. Dian and Rini sit on the porch. Rini asks about Dian's family, and the conversation is ngoko from start to finish.

lines.speaker: Rini:
lines.id: How many brothers and sisters do you have?

lines.speaker: Dian:
lines.text: Loro. Aku duwé kakang siji lan adhi siji.
lines.id: Two. I have an older brother and a younger sister.
lines.literal: two. I have older-brother one and younger-sibling one.

lines.speaker: Rini:
lines.id: Is your little one a boy or a girl?

lines.speaker: Dian:
lines.id: A girl. Her name's Sari, she's still at school.

lines.speaker: Rini:
lines.id: Are your mom and dad in Jakarta too?

lines.speaker: Dian:
lines.text: Iya. Bapakku guru, ibuku dodolan ing pasar.
lines.id: Yes. My dad's a teacher, my mom sells things at the market.
lines.literal: yes. father-my teacher, mother-my selling at market.

lines.speaker: Rini:
lines.id: Oh, same here. My mom sells things too.

lines.speaker: Dian:
lines.id: And you, do you have brothers or sisters?

lines.speaker: Rini:
lines.text: Isih. Simbah putri isih sehat, manggon ing Klaten.
lines.id: Yes. Grandma is still healthy, she lives in Klaten.
lines.literal: still. grandparent female still healthy, live at Klaten.

notes: **Duwé** (to have) goes straight before the thing owned: *aku duwé buku* (I have a book), *dhèwèké duwé omah* (she has a house). Its krama form is *gadhah*, and for someone highly respected there's the krama inggil (honorific) form *kagungan* — *Bapak kagungan mobil* (Father has a car).

**Lanang** and **wédok** are "male" and "female" for people in ngoko. The krama forms are *jaler* and *èstri*. The ngoko words are also used for animals; but calling people *jaler/èstri* in casual chat sounds like filling in a form.
**Isih** means "still", krama *taksih*: *isih sekolah* (still at school), *isih ana* (still there, still alive), *isih adoh* (still far).
**Jenengé Sari** — the ending *-é* here means "her": **her** name is Sari. The same ending also means "the", and context tells them apart.

**Apa** in the middle of a sentence means "or": *lanang apa wédok?* (boy or girl?). So *apa* has three jobs — "what", "or", and a yes/no question marker at the start of a sentence (*apa kowé wis mangan?*, have you eaten?). Its krama form is *punapa* for all three.

**Simbah** means grandfather or grandmother. To specify: *simbah kakung* (grandfather) and *simbah putri* (grandmother). *Kakung* and *putri* are the polite markers for male and female, and they turn up in other forms of address too.
**Padha** means "same" — *wah, padha* is the natural reaction when you find something in common. It also marks a plural doer, as in *padha mangan* (they all eat). Krama: *sami*.

grammars.title: Three possessive endings, and what happens in krama
body: In ngoko, possession works with endings stuck to the noun: *omahku* = house-my. Watch the right-hand column: in krama, two of the three endings **come off and become separate words**.
after: **-é** versus **-né** depends only on the last letter: words ending in a **consonant** take *-é* (*lawang* → *lawangé*, *anak* → *anaké*), words ending in a **vowel** take *-né* (*buku* → *bukuné*, *méja* → *méjané*).

In krama, *-é/-né* becomes **-ipun** (after a consonant) or **-nipun** (after a vowel): *lawangipun*, *bukunipun*. This is one of the most regular swaps in all of Javanese — learn it once, use it everywhere.

To say something belongs to **a named person**, put the name after the thing, with *-é/-né* on the thing: *omahé Rini* (Rini's house), *bukuné Dian* (Dian's book), *anaké Pak Broto* (Mr. Broto's child). Javanese almost always includes that *-é/-né*.

blocks.text: Notice that the words for your own parents and someone else's parents **sit at different levels**. When talking about your own father to someone you respect, you still say *bapak*; when talking about **that person's** father, you go up to *rama*.

blocks.title: Mas, Mbak, Pak, Bu — the titles you must use
items: Javanese people rarely call someone by their bare name. They use **title + name**: *Mas Ahmad*, *Mbak Rini*, *Pak Broto*, *Bu Sri*. Calling out just "Rini!" to someone you don't know well sounds rude.

**Mas** for a man your age or a bit older; **Mbak** for a woman your age or a bit older; **Dhik** or **Dik** for someone younger; **Pak** (sir) and **Bu** (ma'am) for someone much older or in a senior position.
If you're unsure between *Mas* and *Pak*, choose **Pak**. Going one step too high just makes people smile; going one step too low offends.

blocks.text: These questions will come at you, not just from you. Asking about family, home town and marital status is normal small talk in Java — not nosiness but a way of showing interest. Preparing your answers is more useful than memorizing the questions.

blocks.title: An important difference: duwé, ana, and the possessive
items: *Iki bukuku* — this is **my** book (naming the owner). No verb needed at all.
Beginners mix these up. *Aku ana buku* is wrong and sounds odd. For "have", use *duwé*.
